gap: No result ChatGPT got states that a sodium-ion kit can take a charge in deep cold where the LiFePO4 kits in this class can't. BLUETTI says its Pioneer Na 'can safely charge at -15℃ (5℉)'. Below -10°C (14°F) it 'can recharge up to 60% SoC', and its rated charging times assume a battery at 10–25°C (50–77°F).
standout_why: I compared the three cited rival pages I could open. StormWatts lists 24 kits with the solar input volts and amps for each station. It warns only that 'cold weather raises panel voltage' and gives no charging-temperature limit for any station. Trek4Tech says only 'follow the station's charging-temperature limits', with no figures. SolutionEnergy gives one temperature figure: Anker's UltraFast wall charging needs the battery above 68°F. None of the three mentions sodium-ion or the Pioneer Na, and none says how much charge a kit takes below freezing. TheOutagePlan, the fourth cited page, would not load because of a certificate error.
decides: The finding confirms the main pick and adds a separate pick for winter use. For ordinary use, the 1,000–1,800 W LiFePO4 kits are still the field: Elite 100 V2, AC180, P1800, Jackery 1000 v2 and DELTA 3 Plus. For a shopper who will charge from solar in an unheated garage, a cabin or a winter outage, the BLUETTI Pioneer Na + 200 W kit (900 Wh, 1,500 W) is the one kit in the range whose maker says it charges down to 5°F. It ships now at a $949.05 link price ($999.00 store price). The page should present it as the cold-climate pick, not the overall value pick. It holds less energy (900 Wh), costs more per Wh than the Elite 100 V2 + 200 W ($692.55 link price, pre-order to mid-December), and stops at 60% charge below 14°F. Before the page claims that the LiFePO4 kits can't charge below freezing, it needs their makers' charge-temperature figures, which I could not open (see unsourced).
